Okay, give me one word built from chron, meaning time.
Okay, give me one word built from caus or cus, meaning cause.

words_to_read_review.notes:
1. READ: "Okay, if your birthday is in summer - December, January or February - read row 1."
2. READ: "Autumn birthdays - March, April or May - read row 2."
3. READ: "Winter birthdays - June, July or August - read row 3."
4. READ: "Spring birthdays - September, October or November - read row 4."
5. READ: "Everyone reads row 5." Every student reads at least two rows in the group round.
6. ASK: "caus and cus mean cause. Which five words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: accusation, causal, because, excusable, unexcused.
7. ASK: "pend and pens mean hang or pay. Which two words carry them?" 5 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: pendulum, suspense.
8. ASK: "jur, jud and just mean right or law. Which two words carry them?" 5 sec, choral response. EXPECT: jury, injustice.
9. ASK: "Which word names the swinging weight inside an old clock?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: pendulum.
10. ASK: "Which word might you hear in a courtroom when someone is blamed?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: accusation.
11. ASK: "chron means time. Which word names a record of events in time order?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: chronicle.
12. ASK: "What is the opposite of victorious?" 3 sec, choral response. EXPECT: defeated. ACCEPT: beaten.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The strong wind was the cause of the fallen branch on our oval.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: caus is the root on its own here. What question does a cause always answer?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The question why. Why did the branch fall? Because the wind caused it.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Please do not accuse your partner before you check the facts.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. Where does an accuser point the cause?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Straight at another person. To accuse someone is to say they caused the problem.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: My excuse for the late library book was that it slid behind the couch.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. What job is an excuse trying to do for you?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It gives a cause that gets you out of trouble. The ex part means out.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Scientists study causation to find out what really makes a disease spread.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: caus means cause. So what is the difference between a cause and causation?
words_to_spell_review.answer: A cause is the thing itself. Causation is the act of one thing making another happen.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The new scoreboard was too expensive for our school to buy this year.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pens means pay. Which taught ending tells you what the scoreboard is like?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ive ending, the same one in active. Expensive means it makes you pay out a lot.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our opponent in the netball final had the tallest goal shooter in the league.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pon means place. Why is opponent a good word for the other team?
words_to_spell_review.answer: They are placed against you. The op part means against, so they stand in your way.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Year 6 camp gives everyone a taste of independence away from home.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend means hang. Who are you not hanging on when you show independence?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Your parents, or anyone else. You are doing it yourself, not hanging on someone for help.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Rain made us postpone the cross country until next Friday.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which taught prefix tells you the race moves later, not earlier?
words_to_spell_review.answer: post-, meaning after. The race is placed after the date we planned.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Judging a new student by their shoes is a kind of prejudice.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pre means before. So when does prejudice make its judgement?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Before knowing the facts. The judging comes first, and the facts never get a turn.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Mia argued with such conviction that the whole class voted for her plan.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: vict means conquer. What did Mia's conviction conquer?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Everyone's doubts. She was so sure of her plan that the class was won over.

words_to_read_new.meaning: hyper means over + active: active over and above the usual amount
hyper means above + sonic means to do with sound: above the speed of sound
hyper means over + tension means pressure: pressure over the healthy level
hyper means over + bole means throw: words thrown over the top
hyper means over + link: a link that jumps you over to another page
hyper means above + space: a space above and beyond ordinary space
hyper means over + extend means stretch out: to stretch a joint out over its limit
hyper means over + market: a market over the size of a supermarket
hyper means over + focus: focus over the usual amount

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, learn hyper once and you can read a whole family of science, tech and sport words, from hypersonic jets to a hyperextended knee."
READ each word as it appears, then connect hyper to the card meaning: over, above.
hyperactive - hyper means over + active: active over and above the usual amount. A puppy that never stops.
hypersonic - hyper means above + sonic means to do with sound: above the speed of sound. At least five times faster.
hypertension - hyper means over + tension means pressure: pressure over the healthy level. Doctors say it about blood pressure.
hyperbole - hyper means over + bole means throw: words thrown over the top. I have told you a million times!
hyperlink - hyper means over + link: a link that jumps you over to another page.
hyperspace - hyper means above + space: a space above and beyond ordinary space. Science fiction loves it.
hyperextend - hyper means over + extend means stretch out: to stretch a joint out over its limit. A sport injury.
hypermarket - hyper means over + market: a market over the size of a supermarket. Super means above, and hyper goes over even that.
hyperfocus - hyper means over + focus: focus over the usual amount, so you notice nothing else.
Memory hook: hyper is the high jumper sailing OVER the bar. Swap hyper for 'over the' and read the rest: hyperactive is over the active line. Challenge: find a hyper word in a game, ad or sports report by Thursday.
sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, write one sentence that shows what hypertension does to a body."
2. CHECK: the sentence must show the pressure is over the healthy level, not just use the word.
EXTENSION: Build a three-part hyper word from parts you know, then write its full morpheme sum and its meaning.
Answer: e.g. hypertensive = hyper (over) + tense (stretched tight) + -ive (relating to): relating to blood pressure over the healthy level.

new_morph_activity.title: Build the hyper word
new_morph_activity.rule: Join hyper (over, above) to each word. Write the whole new word.
new_morph_activity.example:
One done for you:
hyper + active = hyperactive
items: 1. hyper + link = ?      2. hyper + space = ?
3. hyper + market = ?      4. hyper + extend + -ed = ?
new_morph_activity.footer: Check: is hyper glued on, no gap?
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: 1 hyperlink, 2 hyperspace, 3 hypermarket, 4 hyperextended.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one first. Hyper plus active is hyperactive, written as one word with no gap."
2. SAY: "Now join hyper to each word on your whiteboard. Three minutes, then write it... chin it... show me."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "say hyper out loud, then say the word straight after it. Now write exactly what you just said." Then do number 1 together.
4. SCAN all boards. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> build number 4 together on the board, then re-ask.
TRAP: leaving a gap or a hyphen after hyper. Fix: say hyper is glued on, student rewrites it as one word.
EXTENSION: Write hypermarket and supermarket in one sentence that shows which store is bigger and why.
HELP: Give the four answers jumbled; students match each answer to its sum instead of building it.
---
Purpose: day one joins today's morpheme to words students already own; hyper is the only part they supply. [You Do | Word building | Morphology]
ANSWERS:
1. hyper + link = hyperlink
2. hyper + space = hyperspace
3. hyper + market = hypermarket
4. hyper + extend + -ed = hyperextended
EXTENSION: e.g. The hypermarket is even bigger than the supermarket, because hyper means over and super only means above.

review.notes:
Why learned: the y is the only vowel letter in the word and says a short /i/, and the h behind the r is silent too.
Say it: RITH-uhm, two beats. Write rhy - thm, then check the h behind the r.
Link: every poem and every song has a rhythm, so you will write it in English and in music.

Why learned: the th in the middle says nothing at all, so two letters are silent passengers.
Say it: AS-muh, two beats. Write as - th - ma in three chunks and leave the th in the middle.
Link: asthma turns up in every health and PE unit, and on the sport permission notes you take home.

new.notes:
Why learned: busi is really busy with its y changed to i, so the u says /i/ just like in busy, and the i makes no sound at all.
Say it: BIZ-nis, two beats. Write busi - ness and think busy plus ness.
Link: a business is where people are busy at work. We will use it in maths this term when we plan budgets and work with money.
You will write this word whenever you write about shops, jobs or money, and in any argument about a local business.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Swap vague nouns like stuff, things and people for nouns that name exactly who or what.
WHY THIS WEEK: students' arguments say things like stuff is bad for animals, so the reader has nothing to picture and no reason to care.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: a noun names a person, place or thing. Upgrading swaps a vague noun for an exact one or a stronger one, or builds it into a noun group.

i_do.title: Swap the vague noun
i_do.rule: Upgrade a vague noun to one that names exactly who or what.
i_do.example:
Stuff in the yard hurts animals.
Litter in the yard hurts possums.
items: Vague nouns: stuff, things, people, place.
Ask: exactly who or what?
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: a noun with real strength
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: stuff becomes litter and animals becomes possums - both now name exactly what.
1. SAY: "Okay, in an argument your reader has to picture the problem. Vague nouns like stuff and things give them nothing to picture."
2. WRITE: copy "Stuff in the yard hurts animals." on the class board. POINT at stuff and ask aloud, exactly what stuff?
3. WRITE: cross out stuff and write litter above it, then cross out animals and write possums, so the board reads the upgraded sentence.
4. ASK: "Which sentence makes you picture the problem? Thumbs up for the second, down for the first, on three." 5 sec, voices off. EXPECT: thumbs up - litter and possums name exactly what.
TRAP: adding describing words but keeping the vague noun, like really bad stuff. Fix: say the noun itself must change, student swaps stuff for litter.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether animals is wrong, say it is not wrong, just vague - possums names exactly which animals, so the reader cares more.
---
Purpose: day one shows the exact-noun upgrade on one argument sentence. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: a vague noun could mean almost anything (stuff, things, people); an exact noun lets the reader picture it (litter, possums, Year 6 students).

we_do.title: Which noun does the job?
we_do.rule: Pick the sentence whose noun names exactly who or what.
we_do.example:
A) Things in the canteen are unhealthy.
B) Lollies in the canteen are unhealthy.
items: Thumb up = A is stronger. Thumb down = B is stronger.
Then: what did B do that A did not?
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: B - lollies names exactly what; things is vague.
1. SAY: "Okay, two arguments about the canteen. Read both in your head."
2. ASK: "Thumb up if A is stronger, thumb down if B is. Voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: thumbs down - B.
3. ASK: "What did B do that A did not?" 10 sec, turn and tell, then cold call one pair to say how they know. EXPECT: B names exactly what - lollies, not things.
4. WRITE: copy A on the class board, cross out Things and write Lollies above it, so the board now matches B.
TRAP: choosing A because it sounds more grown-up. Fix: ask which one you can picture, student votes again.
CLARIFY: if a student says canteen is a noun too, say yes, and it is already exact - we only upgrade the vague ones.
---
Purpose: guided judgement between a vague and an exact noun. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: the test is always the same question - can the reader picture exactly who or what?

you_do.title: Upgrade the vague noun
you_do.rule: Swap each vague noun. Bank: litter, bikes, students, garden
you_do.example:
One done for you:
Stuff on the oval cuts our feet.
-> Glass on the oval cuts our feet.
items: A) Things vanish from the rack.   B) People want a longer lunch.
C) The place needs more water.   D) Stuff blocks the drains.
you_do.footer: Check: can you picture it now?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A bikes, B students, C garden, D litter.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one. Stuff was vague, and glass names exactly what cuts our feet."
2. SAY: "Write A to D in your OG book and rewrite each sentence with the exact noun from the bank. Two minutes, on your own."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "ask yourself, exactly what goes missing from a rack at school? Your answer is in the bank." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> do B together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: writing the bank word next to the vague noun, like things bikes. Fix: say the exact noun replaces the vague one, student crosses out and rewrites.
EXTENSION: Write two sentences arguing for a longer lunch with no vague nouns, then swap one exact noun for an even more exact one and explain why it is stronger.
HELP: Give each sentence with only two choices (bikes or garden) so students choose instead of search.
---
Purpose: independent exact-noun swaps with a bank; production is the extension. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) Things vanish from the rack. = Bikes vanish from the rack.
B) People want a longer lunch. = Students want a longer lunch.
C) The place needs more water. = The garden needs more water.
D) Stuff blocks the drains. = Litter blocks the drains.
EXTENSION: e.g. Year 6 students need a longer lunch. Our footy games end before the second half. More exact: Year 6 netballers - it names who is missing out.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - upgrade the vague noun
you_do.check_rule: Tick each exact noun. Fix any sentence that is different.
check_items: A) Bikes vanish from the rack. (things -> bikes)
B) Students want a longer lunch. (people -> students)
C) The garden needs more water. (place -> garden)
D) Litter blocks the drains. (stuff -> litter)
you_do.check_footer: Editing move: circle stuff and things.
you_do.check_notes:
ANSWER: A bikes, B students, C garden, D litter.
1. MODEL: "For A I asked, exactly what vanishes from a rack? A rack holds bikes, so bikes replaces things."
2. SAY: "Now tick each sentence that matches. Fix any that is different, then read it again."
3. ASK: "Which of these four upgrades would make the principal act fastest, and why?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: any with a reason, such as D because blocked drains flood the yard.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> redo C together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "When you edit your next argument, circle every stuff, things and people, and swap each one for exactly who or what."
TRAP: ticking a sentence that still says things. Fix: say the vague noun must be gone, student rewrites it.
---
Purpose: protected reveal that models the exact-noun question and sends it into their own writing. [You Do | Feedback | Grammar | HITS 5]

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The referee made an accusation that our team had wasted time.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: cus means cause. What is the difference between accuse and an accusation?
words_to_spell_review.answer: To accuse is the action. An accusation is the thing you say when you do it - the blame itself.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: We stayed inside at lunch because the oval was flooded.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of because tells you it is about a reason?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The cause part. Because always brings in the cause, so the next words explain why.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Scientists hunt for the causative germ when a bug spreads through a school.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: caus means cause. Which taught ending tells you this germ is like a cause?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ive ending, meaning relating to, the same one in active. The causative germ is the one doing the causing.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: My nan wears a silver pendant shaped like a koala.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: pend means hang. Which taught ending tells you a pendant is the thing that hangs?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ant ending, meaning that which, the same one in assistant. A pendant is that which hangs on a chain.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The postponement of sports day disappointed the whole school.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: post- means after. What did the postponement do to sports day?
words_to_spell_review.answer: It placed the day after the date we planned. Pon means place, so the whole day was moved later.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: The principal will countermand the order to play outside if lightning starts.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: mand means order. Which taught prefix tells you the new order goes against the old one?
words_to_spell_review.answer: counter-, meaning against, the same one in counterattack. To countermand is to give an order against your own order.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our class debate was about justice for animals kept in tiny cages.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: just means right or law. Which taught ending turns it into a state?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The -ice ending, the same one in service. Justice is the state of things being right and fair.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Our class chronicle records every excursion we went on this year.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: chron means time. Why does a chronicle need dates?
words_to_spell_review.answer: Because it records events in time order. Without dates, the reader cannot follow what came first.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: My grandpa takes a tablet every morning for his hypertension.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part of hypertension tells you the pressure is too high?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The hyper part, meaning over. The tension in his blood is over the healthy level.

words_to_spell_review.sentence: Netballers land with bent knees so they do not hyperextend a joint.
words_to_spell_review.prompt: Which part tells you the knee goes past the point where it should stop?
words_to_spell_review.answer: The hyper part, meaning over. The joint stretches out over its normal limit, and that hurts.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect hyper to the card meaning: over, above.
hyperactive - hyper means over + active: active over and above the usual amount.
hyperbole - hyper means over + bole means throw: words thrown over the top. I am so hungry I could eat a horse!
hypersonic - hyper means above + sonic means to do with sound: above the speed of sound.

hypertensive - hyper means over + tense means stretched tight + -ive means relating to: relating to pressure stretched over the healthy level.

sessions.extension:
1. SAY: "Okay, when you finish, use two of the spelling words in one sentence that starts with a subordinate clause."
2. REMIND: a subordinate clause starts with a trigger word like when, because or although, and cannot stand alone. A comma follows it at the front.
EXTENSION: Then move the subordinate clause to the end of the sentence and fix the punctuation.
Answer: e.g. When I am hyperfocused on a game, I miss the hyperlinked homework. / I miss the hyperlinked homework when I am hyperfocused on a game.

new_morph_activity.title: What does the hyper word mean?
new_morph_activity.rule: Write each sum and meaning. Parts: sonic (sound), mobile (moving)
new_morph_activity.example:
One done for you:
hyperactive = hyper + active:
active over the usual amount
items: 1. hypertension = ?      2. hypersonic = ?
3. hypermobile = ?      4. hyperfocus = ?
new_morph_activity.footer: Check: does your meaning say over?
new_morph_activity.notes:
ANSWER: 1 hyper + tension, 2 hyper + sonic, 3 hyper + mobile, 4 hyper + focus - each meaning uses over or above.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one. Hyperactive splits into hyper and active, and the meaning puts over in front: active over the usual amount."
2. SAY: "In your OG workbook, write each word, its sum, then its meaning. The meanings of sonic and mobile are in the banner. Three minutes, on your own."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "cover hyper with your finger. What word is left? Now say over or above in front of it." Then do number 1 together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> do number 2 together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: writing over tension as the meaning without saying what is over. Fix: ask what is too high, student writes pressure over the healthy level.
EXTENSION: Write the full three-part sum for hypertensive and its meaning, then write one sentence that shows the difference between hypertension and hypertensive.
HELP: Give the four sums already split; students write only the meanings.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Choose a noun whose strength fits the facts - strong enough to make the reader care, never over the top.
WHY THIS WEEK: a weak noun (problem, issue) lets the reader shrug; an over-the-top noun (catastrophe) makes them stop trusting you.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: a noun names a person, place or thing. Upgrading swaps a vague noun for an exact one or a stronger one, or builds it into a noun group.

i_do.title: Pick the noun with power
i_do.rule: Choose a noun strong enough to show how serious the problem is.
i_do.example:
Litter is a problem for our creek.
Litter is a threat to our creek.
items: Weak: issue, problem, thing.
Strong: threat, danger, hazard, disaster.
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: threat - it shows the creek could really be harmed; problem only says something is wrong.
1. SAY: "Okay, yesterday we swapped vague nouns for exact ones. Today the noun also needs the right strength, so your reader feels how serious it is."
2. WRITE: copy "Litter is a problem for our creek." on the class board. POINT at problem and say, problem could mean anything, even something tiny.
3. WRITE: cross out problem and write threat above it, then change for to to, so the board reads "Litter is a threat to our creek."
4. ASK: "Which sentence makes you want to do something? Thumbs up for the second, down for the first, on three." 5 sec, voices off. EXPECT: thumbs up - threat shows the creek could be harmed.
TRAP: picking the biggest noun every time. Fix: say the noun must fit the facts, student checks it against what really happens.
CLARIFY: if a student asks why not catastrophe, say too strong becomes hyperbole - over the top - and the reader stops trusting you.
---
Purpose: day two restates the exact-noun rule and adds strength that fits the facts. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: nouns come in strengths - a nuisance, a problem, a hazard, a disaster. The right one is the strongest one the facts can back up.

we_do.title: Too weak or over the top?
we_do.rule: The noun must fit the facts - not too weak, not over the top.
we_do.example: Two wrappers on the oval are a disaster.
items: Thumb up = just right. Thumb down = over the top.
Then: which noun fits two wrappers?
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: over the top - two wrappers are a mess or a nuisance, not a disaster.
1. SAY: "Okay, read the sentence in your head. Is disaster the right strength for two wrappers?"
2. ASK: "Thumb up if it is just right, thumb down if it is over the top. Voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: thumbs down.
3. ASK: "Which noun fits two wrappers better?" 10 sec, turn and tell, then cold call one pair to say how they know. EXPECT: a mess, because it is small and easy to fix. ACCEPT: nuisance, problem.
4. WRITE: copy the sentence on the class board, cross out disaster and write mess above it, so it reads "Two wrappers on the oval are a mess."
TRAP: thinking stronger is always better. Fix: ask what really happens with two wrappers, student picks the noun that matches.
CLARIFY: any mild noun counts - mess, nuisance, problem - as long as it fits two wrappers.
---
Purpose: guided judgement of noun strength against the facts. [We Do | Guided practice | Grammar | HITS 7]
PREP: an over-the-top noun is hyperbole; it is fine in a joke and a weakness in an argument.

you_do.title: Fit the noun to the facts
you_do.rule: Your turn: pick the noun that fits the facts. Write the sentence.
you_do.example:
One done for you:
A wasp nest by the gate is a (worry / hazard).
-> hazard: wasps can sting anyone walking by
items: A) snake in class: pest/danger   B) squeaky chair: nuisance/crisis
C) glass in sandpit: issue/hazard   D) bushfire nearby: mess/emergency
you_do.footer: Check: would the facts back it up?
you_do.notes:
ANSWER: A danger, B nuisance, C hazard, D emergency.
1. SAY: "Okay, look at the finished one. A wasp nest can hurt someone, so hazard fits the facts and worry is too weak."
2. SAY: "Write A to D in your OG book. Pick the noun that fits, then write the whole sentence. Two minutes, on your own."
3. CIRCULATE: to a stuck student say, "picture it happening. Could someone get hurt? If yes, you need the stronger noun." Then do A together.
4. SCAN four books. 80%+ -> reveal the check slide. Less -> do D together on the board, then re-check.
TRAP: choosing crisis for the squeaky chair because it sounds exciting. Fix: ask what really happens, student swaps it for nuisance.
EXTENSION: Write two sentences arguing for a school crossing - one with a noun that is too weak and one that fits - then explain in one line why the second would convince the principal.
HELP: Read each pair aloud and ask, could someone get hurt? Students point to the answer before they write.
---
Purpose: independent choice of noun strength from the facts. [You Do | Independent practice | Grammar | HITS 5]
ANSWERS:
A) A snake in class is a (pest / danger). = danger
B) A squeaky chair is a (nuisance / crisis). = nuisance
C) Glass in the sandpit is an (issue / hazard). = hazard
D) A bushfire nearby is a (mess / emergency). = emergency
EXTENSION: e.g. Cars outside the gate are an issue. / Speeding cars outside the gate are a danger to students. The second names a real risk, so the principal has a reason to act.
you_do.check_title: Tick it or fix it - fit the noun to the facts
you_do.check_rule: Tick each noun that fits. Fix any that is too weak or too strong.
check_items: A) danger - a snake can bite someone
B) nuisance - a squeak annoys, it never hurts
C) hazard - broken glass can cut a hand
D) emergency - a fire near town is serious

you_do.check_notes:

2. SAY: "Now tick each noun that matches. Fix any that is too weak or over the top."
3. ASK: "If the bushfire was already out and far away, which noun would fit then?" 10 sec, turn and tell. EXPECT: a problem, or no longer an emergency - the facts changed, so the strength changes.
4. SCAN corrections. 80%+ -> continue. Less -> redo B together, then re-check.
5. SAY: "When you edit your next argument, read each strong noun and ask, would the facts back this up? If not, tone it down."
TRAP: ticking crisis for the chair. Fix: say a squeak never hurts anyone, student rewrites nuisance.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
SAY: "Okay, some of you may remember omni from earlier in the year. Learn it properly once and you can read words for animals, books, buses and superheroes."
READ each word as it appears, then connect omni to the card meaning: all.
omnibus - omni means all + bus: a vehicle for all the people. Our word bus is just the end of omnibus.
omnivore - omni means all + vore means eating: eating all kinds of food. Plants and meat.
omnivores - omni means all + vore means eating + -s means more than one: more than one animal eating all kinds of food.
omnipresent - omni means all + present means here: present in all places at once.
omnipresence - omni means all + present means here + -ence means the state of: the state of being here in all places at once.
omnishambles - omni means all + shambles means a mess: a mess in all ways. Everything that could go wrong did.
omnium - omni means all + -um, a Latin ending meaning of: the event of all the races. Track cyclists race all of them in one day.
omniscient - omni means all + sci means know + -ent means being: knowing all. A narrator who knows every character's thoughts.
omnipotent - omni means all + pot means power + -ent means being: having all the power.
Memory hook: omni is the big umbrella covering EVERYTHING. Say 'all' in its place - if the word still makes sense, omni is doing its job. Challenge: catch omni in an animal fact or a book blurb before next week.

Answer: e.g. omnipresence = omni (all) + present (here) + -ence (state of): the state of being here in all places. The smell of the sausage sizzle had an omnipresence at the fete.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Build an important noun into a noun group - describers before, a detail after - so the reader sees exactly who or what.
WHY THIS WEEK: one exact noun is good; a built-up noun group lets the reader see the problem and the people it hurts.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: a noun group is the noun plus every word that belongs to it. Students met it in Term 3 Week 1 with prepositional phrases.

i_do.title: Build the noun up
i_do.rule: Build a noun into a noun group: describers before, detail after.
i_do.example:
Students need shade.

items: Before the noun: words that describe it.
After the noun: a where or what-with phrase.
i_do.footer: Tomorrow: all three upgrades at once
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: hot, tired students on the oval - the whole noun group does the arguing.
1. SAY: "Okay, an exact noun on its own can still sound flat. Today you build it up, so your reader sees exactly who needs the shade."
2. WRITE: copy "Students need shade." on the class board. POINT at students and say, this is the noun we will build up.
3. WRITE: add "Hot, tired" in front of students and "on the oval" after it, then underline the whole group, so the board reads "Hot, tired students on the oval need shade."
4. SAY: "Describing words in front, a where phrase after. The whole underlined group is the noun group, and it does the arguing."
TRAP: piling on five describing words. Fix: say two strong ones beat five weak ones, student cuts back to two.
CLARIFY: if a student asks whether on the oval is a phrase, say yes - it is a prepositional phrase telling where, and here it belongs to students.
---

Then add every word that belongs to it.

2. ASK: "What is the noun? Everyone, together, on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: wrappers.
3. ASK: "Now say the whole noun group, every word that belongs to wrappers. Everyone, together, on three." 10 sec. EXPECT: sticky wrappers from the canteen. Then cold call one student to prove from the canteen belongs.

sessions.wtr_new_notes:
READ each word as it appears, then connect omni to the card meaning: all.
omnibus - omni means all + bus: transport for all the people.
omnibuses - omni means all + bus + -es means more than one: more than one vehicle for all the people.
omnivore - omni means all + vore means eating: eating all kinds of food.
omnivores - omni means all + vore means eating + -s means more than one: animals that eat all kinds of food. Possums, magpies and us.
omnivorous - omni means all + vore means eating + -ous means full of: full of eating all kinds of food. The e in vore drops before -ous.
omnipresence - omni means all + present means here + -ence means the state of: the state of being here in all places.
omnishambles - omni means all + shambles means a mess: a mess in all ways.

omniscience - omni means all + sci means know + -ence means the state of: the state of knowing all. Only the narrator has it.
Memory hook: omni is the big umbrella covering EVERYTHING. Say 'all' in its place - if the word still makes sense, omni is doing its job. Challenge: catch omni in an animal fact or a book blurb before next week.

grammar.header_notes:
PURPOSE: Use all three noun upgrades in one argument - exact, the right strength, built up.
WHY THIS WEEK: an argument persuades when the reader can picture the problem and feels how serious it is; this week's three upgrades do exactly that.
ROUTINE: all grammar this week is written in the OG book. No boards - books, thumbs and voices only.
PREP: a noun names a person, place or thing. Upgrading swaps a vague noun for an exact one or a stronger one, or builds it into a noun group.

i_do.title: Three ways to upgrade a noun
i_do.rule: Upgrade nouns three ways: exact, the right strength, built up.
i_do.example:
Stuff by the creek is a problem.
Plastic bottles by the creek are a hazard.
items: Exact: who or what?   Strength: does it fit the facts?
Built up: describer, noun, detail.
i_do.footer: Check: which noun still needs work?
i_do.notes:
ANSWER: stuff -> plastic bottles (exact), problem -> hazard (strength), plastic bottles by the creek (built up).
1. SAY: "Okay, this week's three upgrades all do one job: they make your reader picture the problem and care about it."
2. WRITE: copy "Stuff by the creek is a problem." on the class board. Cross out stuff, write plastic bottles above it, and say: exact - now we know what.
3. WRITE: cross out problem and write hazard, change is to are, then underline plastic bottles by the creek, so the board shows all three upgrades.
4. ASK: "Which upgrade made the biggest difference?" 10 sec, turn and tell, then cold call one pair to convince us. EXPECT: any upgrade with a reason, such as plastic bottles, because you can picture it.
TRAP: forgetting to change is to are once the noun is more than one. Fix: read it aloud, student hears plastic bottles is sounds wrong and fixes it.
CLARIFY: by the creek was already there - it now belongs to the bigger noun group, so the whole group is plastic bottles by the creek.
---
Purpose: day four restates all three upgrades on one argument sentence. [I Do | Explicit modelling | Grammar | HITS 3]
PREP: exact answers who or what, strength answers how serious, and built up adds a describer and a detail around the noun.

we_do.title: Beat the teacher
we_do.rule: I upgraded this argument. Catch the nouns I got wrong.
we_do.example: Things near the canteen bins are a catastrophe.
items: Thumb up = upgraded well. Thumb down = needs work.
Then: which nouns, and what is wrong?
we_do.footer: Stem: That noun is wrong because ...
we_do.notes:
ANSWER: thumbs down - things is still vague and catastrophe is over the top.
1. SAY: "Okay, I tried to upgrade this argument about the canteen bins. Read it in your head and judge my work."
2. ASK: "Thumb up if I upgraded it well, thumb down if it still needs work. Voices off, show me on three." 5 sec. EXPECT: thumbs down.
3. ASK: "Which nouns are wrong, and what is wrong with each?" 10 sec, turn and tell, then cold call one pair to say how they know. EXPECT: things is vague, catastrophe is over the top.
4. WRITE: copy the sentence on the class board, cross out Things and write Wasps, cross out catastrophe and write hazard, so it reads "Wasps near the canteen bins are a hazard."
TRAP: fixing only one noun. Fix: say test every noun with both questions, student finds the second one.
CLARIFY: other exact nouns count too - flies, seagulls, ants - as long as you can picture them near the bins.
